transcript: In the late 1990s, Cisco sat at the heart of the   Internet boom - selling networking  equipment like routers and switches. To demonstrate the Internet's  revolutionary potential,   Cisco made itself into the nimble,  fast-moving corporation of the future. A highly praised e-commerce website.  Rapid, daily financial reports. And   sophisticated data sharing with outsourcing  manufacturers. All made possible with the web. So as the Telecom bubble began to implode, Cisco  management felt confident enough to double down.   They got bullwhipped. In this video, we  look at how Cisco misread the signals. ## Beginnings Cisco Systems' origin story is famous. Leonard "Len" Bosack and Sandra "Sandy" Lerner  first met as masters students at Stanford.   They were kind of opposites  - Sandy aggressive while Len,   rather non-confrontational - but enjoyed  each other's sense of humor and married. After graduating, Sandy became director of  computer facilities at the Stanford business   school and Len, director at the computer  science department. After some time,   the two grew frustrated by a  computer communication issue. The early 1980s saw a Cambrian explosion  of new and different minicomputers and   PCs. Great for competition and variety, but  perhaps not so great for intercommunications. The Stanford campus in 1982 had 5,000 computers  operating within self-contained networks. These   devices can easily communicate with  others within their own network,   but passing data between networks was not so easy. ## A Router Emerges In January 1980, a Stanford  employee named Bill Yeager   working in networking was asked  by his boss to produce something. They wanted to connect together the various  devices in the networks of the Stanford CS and EE   departments as well as the medical center. It was  a mess of incompatible machines like DEC10s, DEC   VAXs, TI Explorers, Symbolics systems, Xerox  PARC Lisp machines, and Alto file servers. In an interview for Network World, Yeager recalls  wiring up those computers and putting together a   special "network operating system" with some  routing code running on a DEC PDP 11/05. Within six months, a working demo of the  router was installed in Pine Hall - midway   between the CS department and the  medical center. Yeager later added   IP and other protocols to turn it  into the first multiprotocol router. Later, he shifted the hardware from the  memory-constrained PDP to a beefier Motorola   68000 circuit board. This was provided to him  by a doctoral student named Andy Bechtolsheim,   who would later use this very type  board to found Sun Microsystems. The product did its job and by 1983,  it was widely adopted across campus.   Len and Sandy realized that this was a  good product to build a company around. In December 1984, they founded Cisco Systems and   later acquired the router technology  and its code for commercialization. ## Starting Out Small Cisco began as a small scrappy business - making a few million dollars a year and  employing relatively few people. Len and Sandy worked 100 hour  weeks - mortgaging their house,   maxing out their credit cards, and taking  a second job to fund this business. At first, Cisco sold its routers  to universities, research centers,   and government facilities. They  worked closely with their customers,   even letting them tinker with the software source  code. Cisco's routers added more protocols and   data transmission standards - becoming a  crucial bridge between various networks. Despite the fast growth however, problems  emerged. Cisco was turning high profits but   somehow remained chronically short in  cash and Sandy's credit cards could no   longer make up the difference. At the  same time, competition was emerging. So Sandy and Len decided to raise venture  capital. After 75+ rejections, Don Valentine,   the legendary general partner of Sequoia  Capital, agreed in 1987 to invest $2.5   million for a 30% stake as well as the  final right to make management decisions. Valentine became Cisco's chairman  - professionalizing its procedures,   bringing in new management  like CEO John Morgridge,   and changing the target customer  from universities to corporations. The business immediately became  successful. Valentine said that   "customers were tearing the hinges  off the door to get the products".   The company didn't even need the $2.5  million in VC money it got from him. But the founders and new managers clashed. The  friction eventually led to Sandy and Len leaving,   and selling their 60+% stake soon  after the company's IPO in 1990.   They then reportedly gave most of the  $170 million they earned to charity. ## Routing the Revolution The company matured at the right time. The 1980s saw the opening up of NSFNET, the  immediate predecessor to the modern Internet.   Built in the hub-and-spoke structure of  feeder networks connected to a central   backbone, NSFNET encourages the  creation of many new networks. As noted by the Computer History  Museum, between 1986 and 1987   the number of Internet hosts across the  world surged from 2,000 to nearly 30,000. At the same time, companies were  buying PCs for workers and networking   them together. They desperately  needed a way to internetwork all   of these local area networks so  their employees can collaborate. Cisco wasn't the only company  with a router-type product.   Others included Proteon, SynOptics,  Banyan, Bridge Communications, and 3Com. But Cisco's routers did the best job of  moving between all these competing network   protocols like DECnet or Xerox's XNS or simple  Internet Protocol or AppleTalk or Novell IPX. Their routers also had the "Internetwork Operating   System" or IOS software. Based  on Yeager's original router code,   IOS was smarter than a simple bridge - which does  not scale - in that it routed traffic in such a   way that sub-networks can remain distinct,  but still connected to the wider world. The company placed IOS at the heart of its  proprietary lock-in strategy - licensing   it to other companies building  networking products or services. Another major sales multiplier  was the Cisco partner program.   This recruited third party distributors  and resellers to sell and support Cisco's   routers. The program amplified the  reach of Cisco's sales network and let   it grow far faster than it could  with only a direct sales force. Sales grew rapidly throughout the early  1990s - encouraged along by smart,   timely acquisitions like the switch  company Crescendo in 1993. In 1991,   they made $183 million. Three years later in  1994, the company cleared $1.2 billion in revenue. Just in case you are wondering like I  was. A switch connects devices within   segments of a single network. A router  forwards data packets along networks.   The two product categories contributed  about two-thirds of Cisco's revenues. Anyway. The next year, John Chambers - a former  IBM and Wang Labs executive - took over as CEO.   He then goes on to aggressively  acquire and integrate literally   dozens of startups to build an  end-to-end networking empire. Between 1993 and 2000, Cisco bought a  staggering 60 startups - paying mostly   in its own stock as the price  soared into the stratosphere. ## The Virtual Corporation Considering Cisco’s central  role in the Internet boom,   the company strove to present  itself as a leader in "e-business". "E-business" back then meant using the  Internet to conduct front and back-end   business processes. John Chambers believed that  the Internet would change how people live, work,   and play - not wrong - and he wanted his  company to be at the forefront of that. Cisco was an early adopter of online purchasing.  They sold product to their thousands of sales   partners through their official website  - titled Cisco Connection Online.   The site began offering simple online  transactions and customer support back in 1994. Then under Chief Information Officer Peter Solvik,   the site was greatly expanded. Thanks to the  power of the Internet, customers can receive   real-time quotes, configure their orders,  and be alerted if their order has any errors. New orders are routed to the right  salesperson over the Internet - saving   the company a reported half a million  dollars a year in FedEx delivery charges. Running on Sun hardware and Solaris, the new  website showed up in 1996 and generated $75   million of sales within its first five months. By  1998, over 65% of Cisco's sales came in through   the website. Customers loved it, and it won  awards from CIO Magazine in 1996, 1997 and 1998. ## Jabil, Solectron and the Assemblers Morgridge and Chambers both believed  in sticking to your core competencies. To them, Cisco's core competencies lay in  corporate strategy, engineering, design, and   customer service. They did not believe that Cisco  can manufacture better than other companies can. So starting in 1992 but continuing  steadily throughout the 1990s,   Cisco outsourced the production of its products to  third party assemblers like Jabil and Solectron. Jabil Circuit is one of the OG assemblers.  Founded by Bill Morean and James Golden in 1966,   the company started off in Detroit fixing circuit  board assemblies for Control Data Systems. In 1979, they struck a turnkey service  partnership with General Motors that   changed their whole future.  They then moved to Florida,   where they picked up a service contract  with IBM to assemble the IBM PC. They expanded their services to include  product design and engineering and went   public in 1993. Since then, they have grown to  become one of the country's largest assemblers. The other major manufacturing partner is  Solectron. Founded in 1977 by Roy Kusumoto   and two Indian Americans as a small assembly  shop, the firm found its initial edge adopting   Total Quality Management and cutting edge  manufacturing like Surface Mounting Technology. Assembly shops and contract manufacturers have  been around in the Silicon Valley for years.   But until the 1990s, they were largely used as  overflow capacity. This was not a pleasant role,   because those orders can get cut for any  reason, leaving the assembler in for a bad time. Then in the late 1980s, former IBM’er Dr.  Koichi Nishimura joined as COO. Nishimura - a   second generation Japanese American who  was interned at Manzanar during World War   II - transformed what was still a local  assembly shop into a globalized giant. Cisco became a major customer of both  Jabil and Solectron. By the late 1990s,   some 70-80% of Cisco's production  was outsourced. It saved them an   estimated 30% on their costs and stood  alongside their control of the IOS   software and the sales partner program  as their key competitive advantages. ## Virtual Close It also let them brag that they had  the best supply chain in the industry. Cisco built an information network - called  an "extranet" - that let them right away   communicate orders and specifications to  their various third-party manufacturers.   Then once the products are built, they  can be shipped directly to the customers. If done right, a Cisco employee never  touches the product. Carl Redfield,   Cisco's SVP of manufacturing said: > We’ve cleaned up the supply chain. You don’t add  value by having multiple people touch a product. Authors described it as like a Japanese  “keiretsu”. A family of companies that   are ostensibly independent of Cisco  but treated as if under their roof.   The extranet - like that rug in the Big  Lebowski - really tied it all together. Cisco vice president Paul  Mountford told CFO Magazine: > Our suppliers can come straight  through and look at our order book,   and then manufacture to the appropriate level It also gave management what seemed  to be an unprecedented real-time view   into demand. Executives can generate  financial reports on the fly showing   the company's total worldwide sales  for the day - and cut by region,   product or customer. It let them perform  daily "tactical operating movements". And then you got the “virtual close”,  a big part of their e-business aura.   CFO Larry Carter would humblebrag in the  Harvard Business Review that they can close   their quarterly accounting books in hours. A  process that took an ordinary company weeks. Anyway. John Chambers called what they had  created a "virtual supply chain" - endowed   with unlimited capacity, outputting extraordinary  reliability, and enabling incredible agility.   It seemed the perfect asset as the  market began to enter a wild boom. ## Raising the Telecom Bubble The Telecoms Act of 1996 remade the telecom  market - opening it up to competition. Also in 1996 and 1997, companies like Amazon  and Yahoo IPO'ed and their stocks soared on   the first day. Their "successes" seemingly  demonstrating the viability of e-commerce,   e-mail, and other e-business. Over 300  Dotcoms stampeded to go public as well. Driven by the belief that the Internet  was going to change everything and myths   like that Internet traffic was doubling  every 100 days, these telecom companies   worked themselves up into a bubble of their own. Entrants like Level 3, Williams and Qwest  raised staggering amounts of money from   the stock and bond markets to build  large-scale Internet infrastructure. In 1995, the year before the new law, the  telecom industry put in $47 billion of   capex. By the peak year 2000, the  SF Federal Reserve estimated that   the telecom capex investment reached about  $120 billion - or about $233 billion today. The telecom bubble deserves more detail,  so let me save that for a future video.   To bring things back to Cisco, these  new telecom firms most often bought   their networking gear from Cisco or its  two major competitors Lucent and Nortel. Lucent and Nortel were larger as measured  by revenue, but it was Cisco that became the   business world’s darling. The staggering sales  and profit growth. The fresh startup smell. The   e-business savvy. If you weren't trying to  be like Cisco, then YOU were falling behind. In 1998, Cisco's market cap reached $100  billion. They achieved that milestone in   just 8 years after their IPO - seven  years faster than it took Mr. Softee. Revenues grew at 50% each year from $8.5 billion  in 1998 to $18.9 billion in 2000. To keep up with   the rapidly changing market, the company bought  even more startups - 17 purchases in 1999 alone. Including shelling out an ankle-breaking  $7 billion to snag a fiber optic startup   called Cerent, which turned only $15  million in revenue. Optics valuations   in the bubble era were as hilarious as a  donkey eating your figs. Just kills me. The frenzy pays off though with a daring  transition. Up until then, most telecoms   carried Internet data over voice circuits.  Cisco feels that this is not the future. Rather,   their vision is a packet-based network that treats  data, voice, and video signals all the same. In 1998, Cisco declares their intention to  build such packet-switched data networks,   including to send those  signals over optical fiber. This puts Lucent and Nortel on their back  foot, and they struggle to make a similar   transition. Lucent tried to bolt it  onto their legacy circuit equipment   while Nortel spent $9 billion to buy Bay  Networks. Neither strategy really works. This leaves Cisco dominant in the  lucrative Internet data networking   field - the clear future of the industry. As the   fiber bubble drove on over the next two  years, Cisco was the clear beneficiary. Solectron benefitted from the bubble frenzy too.  In 1999, they became the world's largest contract   manufacturer with over $8 billion in sales.  Thanks in part to the strategy of acquiring   their customers’ factories, revenues  grew over 50% a year from 1992 to 1999. The business press labeled Solectron  the "Intel" of contract manufacturing.   At the time that was considered high praise. ## Danger Signs The Dotcom Bubble was of course  a bubble, but primarily one in   the stock markets. Most sensible people  recognized that things there were crazy. Telecoms on the other hand seemed  different, because they were   laying down fiber lines. Hard assets.  And for decades, telecom meant AT&T.   Plain Old Telephone Service that is boring  and thus safe to plunge your nest egg into. But that was in the before-times. People  were slow to catch on to the fact that   the industry really had changed. This  wasn’t your grandpa’s monopoly, anymore. Moreover, few noticed that the  fiber everyone was building out   was duplicative. Level 3 and Qwest and their  peers focused on building out the easy stuff:   Long-distance fiber loops  cutting through rural areas. Far fewer dollars were being spent on the  "last mile" connections actually going into   people's homes. Because unfortunately that  was the hardest part. For every dollar spent   laying down long-distance cable, twenty  dollars must be spent on last mile. There were also the shady vendor financing  practices. If you have read an Nvidia bear   report recently, then you might have heard of  these. Building infrastructure takes a lot of   upfront capital expenditure that can only  be paid back over a long period of time. These telecom startups lacked that kind of  cash flow, so they turned to their own vendors.   Vendors can help startups get off the ground by  directly investing in said startup, accepting   stock in exchange for product, or loaning money  that they can then turn around to buy product. Cisco was actually one of the better actors  in this. By late 2000, Cisco had only $2.4   billion committed, of which $625 million had  been drawn. To compare, Nortel showed about $3   billion in vendor financing commitments and  Lucent a staggering $8.1 billion in total. One superfun example was Winstar  Communications. Between 1995 and 2000,   they raised billions to build the "world's  first global end-to-end broadband network". This included a very unusual $500 million  from Lucent in October 1998 - funding a   staggering 40+% of the price of Lucent equipment.  Traditional norms numbered 10-15% at the most. Some tried to get the word out. Andrew Odlyzko of  AT&T Labs published a paper in late 1998 debunking   the Internet 100-day traffic doubling factoid,  which had by then become fund-raising gospel. A 1999 issue of the McKinsey Quarterly  noted that if all the fiber planned by   the US telcos were to be fully utilized  then US backbone capacity would rise   by 200 times over the next 3-5 years.  They noted significant oversupply then,   but added that there was no technological reason  why that backbone wouldn’t be fully utilized. ## The Orders Are Real In March 2000, Cisco became the world's largest  company with a market cap of $531 billion. The stock had tripled over the past year.  Analysts predicted that the company would be   the first to ever make the trillion dollar market  cap number - driven by the Internet tidal wave. In May 2000, Fortune Magazine called John Chambers  a "money-making machine" and mooted him as the   world's greatest CEO alongside Jack Welch  (ew), Lou Gerstner, and Sony's Nobuyuki Idei. By then, the Dotcom bubble had  already begun to burst. Yet even   as the Dotcoms made their merry  little way to the slaughterhouse,   the telecom bubble continued on. And  in some aspects, it even intensified. For instance in July 2000, Nortel  reported higher profits and - thanks   to all the optical gear customers  were storming to buy - even raised   their sales expectations for the rest of  the year from 35% growth to 40% growth. This final burst of energy created shortages.  In early 2000, Cisco started noticing that   lead times on some of the networking  equipment had grown to four to six months.   Such shortages were estimated to have  cost the company 10% of revenue last year. Trusting their numbers and forecasting  60% revenue growth for the forthcoming   fiscal year starting in July 2000, Cisco went  aggressive. They moved forward on long-term   commitments with its manufacturing  partners and component suppliers. Solectron now faced a dilemma. Its own  internal forecasts looked at the worsening   general economy and preached caution.  They warned Cisco that they were buying   more communications chips, optical lasers and  assembly boards than what seemed necessary. Cisco replied that their business would  keep on growing. Dotcoms were less than   5% of their business. Some Dotcoms still  had money and were still going to buy.   So Cisco was still going to need those extra  components. The WSJ reported Chambers saying: > "To not plan to meet that growth is  the quickest way to lose customers" You can see these start to appear on  Cisco's financial statements. Their Year   2000 10-K - covering the year ended July  2000 - showed inventories rising 87% from   the previous year due to "increased purchases  to secure the supply of certain components". The following 10-Q statement covering the  quarter ending October 2000 showed Cisco's   inventories rising another 58.8%. Again in  part because of further component purchases. ## Mixed Signals So Cisco wasn't backing off. They  were doubling down. And to be fair,   the signs were mixed - especially  in that final quarter of 2000. In that quarter I mentioned earlier ending in  October, Cisco reported record revenue growth   of 65%. Their executives insisted that  they had not seen any sign of a slowdown. But the stock was down 32% from  its March peak. And Wall Street   analysts were now openly saying that the telecom   boom was slowing. The telecom giants were  pulling back on their equipment purchases. And what was especially worrisome was  that the telecom startups were losing   the ability to raise cash to finish their  networks. The first eight months of the year,   telecoms raised $5.6 billion a month  selling stocks and bonds. In September   that fell to just $1.2 billion. October,  $900 million. November, $700 million. Some of those startups were going bankrupt. A  notable one was ICG Communications in Colorado,   which owed Cisco $32 million for equipment. Ominously, Cisco's other partners - not  just Solectron - were revising forecasts.   A notable one was Xilinx - a maker  of FPGA silicon chips that go into   routers. In September 2000, they  cut their internal growth forecasts   from 16-20% to just 10%. Other partners  warned Cisco that shipments were slowing. But just to give you a sense how  hard predicting the future is,   signals were very mixed. Morgan Stanley's  Christopher Stix reported that his own   channel checks still found wait  times of 3 months for Cisco gear. And tens of millions of people were  still joining the Internet every   month. So even if those telecom sales  are indeed slowing, sales in corporate   networking and data-based Internet switches  appeared to have so much runway ahead. The WSJ later reported that Cisco's management  didn't really look at the overall economy or the   cash positions of their telecom customers.  They of course noticed the downturn,   but framed it as a consolidation that will  produce stronger telecom customers in the end. So in the moment, two or three random negative  signals did not seem a big deal. Twice before,   Cisco's management hit the gas rather  than pulling back - like during the   Asian Financial Crisis - and twice before  the gamble paid off. The company had grown   for literally dozens of quarters.  A slowdown did not seem feasible. ## The Dream is Collapsing On December 4th, John Chambers told analysts: > "I have never been more optimistic about the  future of our industry as a whole or of Cisco." About a week later in mid-December 2000,  he ran his daily financial report and   noticed that the day's sales had fallen  short of projections. After the trend   persisted for a week, he got worried  enough to start calling customers. So what was happening? Earlier in the year,   Cisco customers - facing months-long delays  in getting product - started putting down   double and even triple orders to get the  quantities they needed. Cisco salespeople   sometimes added their own "buffer" to  those numbers, hoping to get attention. Sometimes, customers went to multiple resellers  and suppliers - putting orders in with them too.   The result was an exaggerated demand signal that  Cisco took to heart. They faithfully transmitted   that to the rest of the supply chain and  put in big component orders to meet them. When things started to go south later in the  year, all those orders got canceled. Buffers   that the company thought it had - like a massive  $3.8 billion sales backlog in late September,   equivalent to 8-10 weeks of sales -  evaporated like raindrops in Death Valley. The company and wider market initially  held to some hope that things would come   back. News articles mentioning  component shortages for certain   switches impeding sales were still  coming out in early January 2001. But in mid January 2001, Chambers  admitted that the quarter was more   challenging than anticipated due to a  slowdown in customer spending. Cisco   later reported strong revenue growth  numbers but missed its earnings numbers. The company tried to keep a cheery  tone. They emphasized a positive 3-5   year outlook because many businesses still have to   modernize to leverage more Internet. But  in the end, they had to face the music. ## Fallout Two months later in April 2001, Cisco  took responsibility for its bad forecast. They admitted that sales will  fall 30% from the prior quarter,   cut 8,500 jobs, and took an estimated  $2.5 billion financial charge on unused   inventory held by Jabil and Solectron -  including stuff they committed to even   if there wasn't a contract. The actual  number turned out to be $2.2 billion. They sold some of the components. Others, they  warehoused in the hope of the market coming back.   When it didn't, that inventory had to be destroyed  because it had been custom made for Cisco. Cisco's rapid buildup and then abrupt  cut reverberated through its supply   chain partners. In March 2001, Solectron  announced that its revenues had surged 85%   with profits meeting Wall Street's targets. Yet  at the same time they were cutting 8,200 jobs. I did a video about JDS Uniphase - ancestor  to today’s Lumentum - which supplied many of   the optical fiber components like lasers to Cisco  and others. They cut a staggering 16,000 jobs in   2001 alone and a stock price that had once been  over $130 in 2000 spiraled to $7 a year later. In an oral history for the  Computer History Museum,   John Morgridge - the former CEO who  then stepped up to chairman - recalled   seeing the internal trends data  deteriorating in the autumn of 2000. But Chambers was by nature an optimistic guy.  Faced with these numbers, he decided to hit the   pedal just as he did before. And in the end,  the downturn turned out to be far worse than   almost everyone anticipated. Dips happen all the  time. But 2001 and the telecom bubble was special. ## Conclusion Cisco got bullwhipped. The bullwhip  effect is, formally speaking,   a supply chain phenomena where shifts in retail  amplify in size the deeper you go down the chain. I first mentioned it in a prior  video about TSMC and Silicon Valley. The 2000 Cisco inventory write-off is  a particularly pure form of the effect.   A short period of shortages triggered  excessive inventory buildup within the   supply chain. Layers in that chain  amplified those demand signals. Cisco's management then took those signals  to heart - overriding the instincts of their   manufacturing partners, who  are a bit more conservative. Fortunately for Cisco, the company had the  money to weather the storm. They took on their   partners' financial obligations and in doing  so were able to keep the supply chain intact.   And that helped them survive and scale up for  when the downturn finally ended. Unfortunately,   not everyone in that industry had  the money to do what Cisco did.

Just in case you are wondering like I  was. A switch connects devices within
segments of a single network. A router  forwards data packets along networks.
The two product categories contributed  about two-thirds of Cisco's revenues.
Anyway. The next year, John Chambers - a former  IBM and Wang Labs executive - took over as CEO.
He then goes on to aggressively  acquire and integrate literally
dozens of startups to build an  end-to-end networking empire.
Between 1993 and 2000, Cisco bought a  staggering 60 startups - paying mostly
in its own stock as the price  soared into the stratosphere.
## The Virtual Corporation
Considering Cisco’s central  role in the Internet boom,
the company strove to present  itself as a leader in "e-business".
"E-business" back then meant using the  Internet to conduct front and back-end
business processes. John Chambers believed that  the Internet would change how people live, work,
and play - not wrong - and he wanted his  company to be at the forefront of that.
Cisco was an early adopter of online purchasing.  They sold product to their thousands of sales
partners through their official website  - titled Cisco Connection Online.
The site began offering simple online  transactions and customer support back in 1994.
Then under Chief Information Officer Peter Solvik,
the site was greatly expanded. Thanks to the  power of the Internet, customers can receive
real-time quotes, configure their orders,  and be alerted if their order has any errors.
New orders are routed to the right  salesperson over the Internet - saving
the company a reported half a million  dollars a year in FedEx delivery charges.
Running on Sun hardware and Solaris, the new  website showed up in 1996 and generated $75
million of sales within its first five months. By  1998, over 65% of Cisco's sales came in through
the website. Customers loved it, and it won  awards from CIO Magazine in 1996, 1997 and 1998.
## Jabil, Solectron and the Assemblers
Morgridge and Chambers both believed  in sticking to your core competencies.
To them, Cisco's core competencies lay in  corporate strategy, engineering, design, and
customer service. They did not believe that Cisco  can manufacture better than other companies can.
So starting in 1992 but continuing  steadily throughout the 1990s,
Cisco outsourced the production of its products to  third party assemblers like Jabil and Solectron.
Jabil Circuit is one of the OG assemblers.  Founded by Bill Morean and James Golden in 1966,
the company started off in Detroit fixing circuit  board assemblies for Control Data Systems.
In 1979, they struck a turnkey service  partnership with General Motors that
changed their whole future.  They then moved to Florida,
where they picked up a service contract  with IBM to assemble the IBM PC.
They expanded their services to include  product design and engineering and went
public in 1993. Since then, they have grown to  become one of the country's largest assemblers.
The other major manufacturing partner is  Solectron. Founded in 1977 by Roy Kusumoto
and two Indian Americans as a small assembly  shop, the firm found its initial edge adopting
Total Quality Management and cutting edge  manufacturing like Surface Mounting Technology.
Assembly shops and contract manufacturers have  been around in the Silicon Valley for years.
But until the 1990s, they were largely used as  overflow capacity. This was not a pleasant role,
because those orders can get cut for any  reason, leaving the assembler in for a bad time.
Then in the late 1980s, former IBM’er Dr.  Koichi Nishimura joined as COO. Nishimura - a
second generation Japanese American who  was interned at Manzanar during World War
II - transformed what was still a local  assembly shop into a globalized giant.
Cisco became a major customer of both  Jabil and Solectron. By the late 1990s,
some 70-80% of Cisco's production  was outsourced. It saved them an
estimated 30% on their costs and stood  alongside their control of the IOS
software and the sales partner program  as their key competitive advantages.
## Virtual Close
It also let them brag that they had  the best supply chain in the industry.
Cisco built an information network - called  an "extranet" - that let them right away
communicate orders and specifications to  their various third-party manufacturers.
Then once the products are built, they  can be shipped directly to the customers.
If done right, a Cisco employee never  touches the product. Carl Redfield,
Cisco's SVP of manufacturing said:
> We’ve cleaned up the supply chain. You don’t add  value by having multiple people touch a product.
Authors described it as like a Japanese  “keiretsu”. A family of companies that
are ostensibly independent of Cisco  but treated as if under their roof.
The extranet - like that rug in the Big  Lebowski - really tied it all together.
Cisco vice president Paul  Mountford told CFO Magazine:
> Our suppliers can come straight  through and look at our order book,
and then manufacture to the appropriate level
It also gave management what seemed  to be an unprecedented real-time view
into demand. Executives can generate  financial reports on the fly showing
the company's total worldwide sales  for the day - and cut by region,
product or customer. It let them perform  daily "tactical operating movements".
And then you got the “virtual close”,  a big part of their e-business aura.
CFO Larry Carter would humblebrag in the  Harvard Business Review that they can close
their quarterly accounting books in hours. A  process that took an ordinary company weeks.
Anyway. John Chambers called what they had  created a "virtual supply chain" - endowed
with unlimited capacity, outputting extraordinary  reliability, and enabling incredible agility.
It seemed the perfect asset as the  market began to enter a wild boom.
## Raising the Telecom Bubble
The Telecoms Act of 1996 remade the telecom  market - opening it up to competition.
Also in 1996 and 1997, companies like Amazon  and Yahoo IPO'ed and their stocks soared on
the first day. Their "successes" seemingly  demonstrating the viability of e-commerce,
e-mail, and other e-business. Over 300  Dotcoms stampeded to go public as well.
Driven by the belief that the Internet  was going to change everything and myths
like that Internet traffic was doubling  every 100 days, these telecom companies
worked themselves up into a bubble of their own.
Entrants like Level 3, Williams and Qwest  raised staggering amounts of money from
the stock and bond markets to build  large-scale Internet infrastructure.
In 1995, the year before the new law, the  telecom industry put in $47 billion of
capex. By the peak year 2000, the  SF Federal Reserve estimated that
the telecom capex investment reached about  $120 billion - or about $233 billion today.
The telecom bubble deserves more detail,  so let me save that for a future video.
To bring things back to Cisco, these  new telecom firms most often bought
their networking gear from Cisco or its  two major competitors Lucent and Nortel.
Lucent and Nortel were larger as measured  by revenue, but it was Cisco that became the
business world’s darling. The staggering sales  and profit growth. The fresh startup smell. The
e-business savvy. If you weren't trying to  be like Cisco, then YOU were falling behind.
In 1998, Cisco's market cap reached $100  billion. They achieved that milestone in
just 8 years after their IPO - seven  years faster than it took Mr. Softee.
Revenues grew at 50% each year from $8.5 billion  in 1998 to $18.9 billion in 2000. To keep up with
the rapidly changing market, the company bought  even more startups - 17 purchases in 1999 alone.
Including shelling out an ankle-breaking  $7 billion to snag a fiber optic startup
called Cerent, which turned only $15  million in revenue. Optics valuations
in the bubble era were as hilarious as a  donkey eating your figs. Just kills me.
The frenzy pays off though with a daring  transition. Up until then, most telecoms
carried Internet data over voice circuits.  Cisco feels that this is not the future. Rather,
their vision is a packet-based network that treats  data, voice, and video signals all the same.
In 1998, Cisco declares their intention to  build such packet-switched data networks,
including to send those  signals over optical fiber.
This puts Lucent and Nortel on their back  foot, and they struggle to make a similar
transition. Lucent tried to bolt it  onto their legacy circuit equipment
while Nortel spent $9 billion to buy Bay  Networks. Neither strategy really works.
This leaves Cisco dominant in the  lucrative Internet data networking
field - the clear future of the industry. As the
fiber bubble drove on over the next two  years, Cisco was the clear beneficiary.
Solectron benefitted from the bubble frenzy too.  In 1999, they became the world's largest contract
manufacturer with over $8 billion in sales.  Thanks in part to the strategy of acquiring
their customers’ factories, revenues  grew over 50% a year from 1992 to 1999.
The business press labeled Solectron  the "Intel" of contract manufacturing.
At the time that was considered high praise.
## Danger Signs
The Dotcom Bubble was of course  a bubble, but primarily one in
the stock markets. Most sensible people  recognized that things there were crazy.
Telecoms on the other hand seemed  different, because they were
laying down fiber lines. Hard assets.  And for decades, telecom meant AT&T.
Plain Old Telephone Service that is boring  and thus safe to plunge your nest egg into.
But that was in the before-times. People  were slow to catch on to the fact that
the industry really had changed. This  wasn’t your grandpa’s monopoly, anymore.
Moreover, few noticed that the  fiber everyone was building out
was duplicative. Level 3 and Qwest and their  peers focused on building out the easy stuff:
Long-distance fiber loops  cutting through rural areas.
Far fewer dollars were being spent on the  "last mile" connections actually going into
people's homes. Because unfortunately that  was the hardest part. For every dollar spent
laying down long-distance cable, twenty  dollars must be spent on last mile.
There were also the shady vendor financing  practices. If you have read an Nvidia bear
report recently, then you might have heard of  these. Building infrastructure takes a lot of
upfront capital expenditure that can only  be paid back over a long period of time.
These telecom startups lacked that kind of  cash flow, so they turned to their own vendors.
Vendors can help startups get off the ground by  directly investing in said startup, accepting
stock in exchange for product, or loaning money  that they can then turn around to buy product.
Cisco was actually one of the better actors  in this. By late 2000, Cisco had only $2.4
billion committed, of which $625 million had  been drawn. To compare, Nortel showed about $3
billion in vendor financing commitments and  Lucent a staggering $8.1 billion in total.
One superfun example was Winstar  Communications. Between 1995 and 2000,
they raised billions to build the "world's  first global end-to-end broadband network".
This included a very unusual $500 million  from Lucent in October 1998 - funding a
staggering 40+% of the price of Lucent equipment.  Traditional norms numbered 10-15% at the most.
Some tried to get the word out. Andrew Odlyzko of  AT&T Labs published a paper in late 1998 debunking
the Internet 100-day traffic doubling factoid,  which had by then become fund-raising gospel.
A 1999 issue of the McKinsey Quarterly  noted that if all the fiber planned by
the US telcos were to be fully utilized  then US backbone capacity would rise
by 200 times over the next 3-5 years.  They noted significant oversupply then,
but added that there was no technological reason  why that backbone wouldn’t be fully utilized.
## The Orders Are Real
In March 2000, Cisco became the world's largest  company with a market cap of $531 billion.
The stock had tripled over the past year.  Analysts predicted that the company would be
the first to ever make the trillion dollar market  cap number - driven by the Internet tidal wave.
In May 2000, Fortune Magazine called John Chambers  a "money-making machine" and mooted him as the
world's greatest CEO alongside Jack Welch  (ew), Lou Gerstner, and Sony's Nobuyuki Idei.
By then, the Dotcom bubble had  already begun to burst. Yet even
as the Dotcoms made their merry  little way to the slaughterhouse,
the telecom bubble continued on. And  in some aspects, it even intensified.
For instance in July 2000, Nortel  reported higher profits and - thanks
to all the optical gear customers  were storming to buy - even raised
their sales expectations for the rest of  the year from 35% growth to 40% growth.
This final burst of energy created shortages.  In early 2000, Cisco started noticing that
lead times on some of the networking  equipment had grown to four to six months.
Such shortages were estimated to have  cost the company 10% of revenue last year.
Trusting their numbers and forecasting  60% revenue growth for the forthcoming
fiscal year starting in July 2000, Cisco went  aggressive. They moved forward on long-term
commitments with its manufacturing  partners and component suppliers.
Solectron now faced a dilemma. Its own  internal forecasts looked at the worsening
general economy and preached caution.  They warned Cisco that they were buying
more communications chips, optical lasers and  assembly boards than what seemed necessary.
Cisco replied that their business would  keep on growing. Dotcoms were less than
5% of their business. Some Dotcoms still  had money and were still going to buy.
So Cisco was still going to need those extra  components. The WSJ reported Chambers saying:
> "To not plan to meet that growth is  the quickest way to lose customers"
You can see these start to appear on  Cisco's financial statements. Their Year
2000 10-K - covering the year ended July  2000 - showed inventories rising 87% from
the previous year due to "increased purchases  to secure the supply of certain components".
The following 10-Q statement covering the  quarter ending October 2000 showed Cisco's
inventories rising another 58.8%. Again in  part because of further component purchases.
## Mixed Signals
So Cisco wasn't backing off. They  were doubling down. And to be fair,
the signs were mixed - especially  in that final quarter of 2000.
In that quarter I mentioned earlier ending in  October, Cisco reported record revenue growth
of 65%. Their executives insisted that  they had not seen any sign of a slowdown.
But the stock was down 32% from  its March peak. And Wall Street
analysts were now openly saying that the telecom
boom was slowing. The telecom giants were  pulling back on their equipment purchases.
And what was especially worrisome was  that the telecom startups were losing
the ability to raise cash to finish their  networks. The first eight months of the year,
telecoms raised $5.6 billion a month  selling stocks and bonds. In September
that fell to just $1.2 billion. October,  $900 million. November, $700 million.
Some of those startups were going bankrupt. A  notable one was ICG Communications in Colorado,
which owed Cisco $32 million for equipment.
Ominously, Cisco's other partners - not  just Solectron - were revising forecasts.
A notable one was Xilinx - a maker  of FPGA silicon chips that go into
routers. In September 2000, they  cut their internal growth forecasts
from 16-20% to just 10%. Other partners  warned Cisco that shipments were slowing.
But just to give you a sense how  hard predicting the future is,
signals were very mixed. Morgan Stanley's  Christopher Stix reported that his own
channel checks still found wait  times of 3 months for Cisco gear.
And tens of millions of people were  still joining the Internet every
month. So even if those telecom sales  are indeed slowing, sales in corporate
networking and data-based Internet switches  appeared to have so much runway ahead.
The WSJ later reported that Cisco's management  didn't really look at the overall economy or the
cash positions of their telecom customers.  They of course noticed the downturn,
but framed it as a consolidation that will  produce stronger telecom customers in the end.
So in the moment, two or three random negative  signals did not seem a big deal. Twice before,
Cisco's management hit the gas rather  than pulling back - like during the
Asian Financial Crisis - and twice before  the gamble paid off. The company had grown
for literally dozens of quarters.  A slowdown did not seem feasible.
## The Dream is Collapsing On December 4th, John Chambers told analysts:
> "I have never been more optimistic about the  future of our industry as a whole or of Cisco."
About a week later in mid-December 2000,  he ran his daily financial report and
noticed that the day's sales had fallen  short of projections. After the trend
persisted for a week, he got worried  enough to start calling customers.
So what was happening? Earlier in the year,
Cisco customers - facing months-long delays  in getting product - started putting down
double and even triple orders to get the  quantities they needed. Cisco salespeople
sometimes added their own "buffer" to  those numbers, hoping to get attention.
Sometimes, customers went to multiple resellers  and suppliers - putting orders in with them too.
The result was an exaggerated demand signal that  Cisco took to heart. They faithfully transmitted
that to the rest of the supply chain and  put in big component orders to meet them.
When things started to go south later in the  year, all those orders got canceled. Buffers
that the company thought it had - like a massive  $3.8 billion sales backlog in late September,
equivalent to 8-10 weeks of sales -  evaporated like raindrops in Death Valley.
The company and wider market initially  held to some hope that things would come
back. News articles mentioning  component shortages for certain
switches impeding sales were still  coming out in early January 2001.
But in mid January 2001, Chambers  admitted that the quarter was more
challenging than anticipated due to a  slowdown in customer spending. Cisco
later reported strong revenue growth  numbers but missed its earnings numbers.
The company tried to keep a cheery  tone. They emphasized a positive 3-5
year outlook because many businesses still have to
modernize to leverage more Internet. But  in the end, they had to face the music.
## Fallout
Two months later in April 2001, Cisco  took responsibility for its bad forecast.
They admitted that sales will  fall 30% from the prior quarter,
cut 8,500 jobs, and took an estimated  $2.5 billion financial charge on unused
inventory held by Jabil and Solectron -  including stuff they committed to even
if there wasn't a contract. The actual  number turned out to be $2.2 billion.
They sold some of the components. Others, they  warehoused in the hope of the market coming back.
When it didn't, that inventory had to be destroyed  because it had been custom made for Cisco.
Cisco's rapid buildup and then abrupt  cut reverberated through its supply
chain partners. In March 2001, Solectron  announced that its revenues had surged 85%
with profits meeting Wall Street's targets. Yet  at the same time they were cutting 8,200 jobs.
I did a video about JDS Uniphase - ancestor  to today’s Lumentum - which supplied many of
the optical fiber components like lasers to Cisco  and others. They cut a staggering 16,000 jobs in
2001 alone and a stock price that had once been  over $130 in 2000 spiraled to $7 a year later.
In an oral history for the  Computer History Museum,
John Morgridge - the former CEO who  then stepped up to chairman - recalled
seeing the internal trends data  deteriorating in the autumn of 2000.
But Chambers was by nature an optimistic guy.  Faced with these numbers, he decided to hit the
pedal just as he did before. And in the end,  the downturn turned out to be far worse than
almost everyone anticipated. Dips happen all the  time. But 2001 and the telecom bubble was special.
## Conclusion
Cisco got bullwhipped. The bullwhip  effect is, formally speaking,
a supply chain phenomena where shifts in retail  amplify in size the deeper you go down the chain.
I first mentioned it in a prior  video about TSMC and Silicon Valley.
The 2000 Cisco inventory write-off is  a particularly pure form of the effect.
A short period of shortages triggered  excessive inventory buildup within the
supply chain. Layers in that chain  amplified those demand signals.
Cisco's management then took those signals  to heart - overriding the instincts of their
manufacturing partners, who  are a bit more conservative.
Fortunately for Cisco, the company had the  money to weather the storm. They took on their
partners' financial obligations and in doing  so were able to keep the supply chain intact.
And that helped them survive and scale up for  when the downturn finally ended. Unfortunately,
not everyone in that industry had  the money to do what Cisco did.
